lines.text: Go on. The bus is not coming and you plainly have questions.
Why close the stop before the building is down?
They did not close it. They removed the number from the pole and left the electricity on.
For a week the buses slowed because people waved. Then the drivers learned not to look at us.

choices.text: Ask when a bus last stopped.

lines.text: Did you complain?
Twice. The first reply said the stop did not exist. The second thanked me for reporting a damaged light at a stop that did not exist.
That is local government achieving a sort of harmony.
When did one last stop here?
Three Thursdays ago. Empty except for the driver. He opened both doors and waited as though somebody had rung the bell.
Nobody got on. That includes me.
What were the baths like?
Blue tile, iron changing stalls, and water cold enough to make children honest.
Ellery bought the pool, roofed half the windows, and called it a rehearsal resource. You could still smell chlorine in the corridor.
Did your daughter come back after Ellery took it over?
Once. She said the deep end was under a floor and somebody had put a piano where the lifeguard chair stood.
She did not like hearing scales come through the drain grilles. Neither did I, after she mentioned it.
Did they warn anyone before they drained it?
They posted the notice inside, after the last public session. You had to enter a closed building to learn the building was closed.
Ellery has always preferred an audience already in the room.
What do you hear from the building at night?
The tower, mostly. Practice carries in wet weather. One bell at a time, then seven answering too late.
Tuesday there was a man counting in the loading yard. He reached four. The next voice began again at one.

choices.text: Ask whether she saw the second man.
Say it was probably a recording.

lines.text: Did you see the other man?
No. I saw one shadow cross the yard each time either voice spoke.
That is not the same answer, I know.
It could have been a recording.
Of course it could. You are carrying the machine that makes that answer useful.
Keep it useful.
Still no 48. Still a light for it. How did Ellery become your problem?

choices.text: Ask if anyone else went in tonight.

lines.text: Has anyone else gone through the gate tonight?
A man in a clean contractor jacket photographed the padlock before dusk. He never opened it.
Your guard watched him leave and then checked the glass as if the reflection had stayed.
If the bus does not stop, why wait here?
My flat is three streets over. Here I can see the baths windows.
Some habits deserve a light, even after the route is gone.
The music school came second. Those rooms at the back were stables, then laundry, then rehearsal rooms nobody could heat.
You knew the place?
Knew the walls. Every Thursday the tower bells shook dust out of my gutter.
Listen past the traffic. The tower always carried farther in wet weather.

lines.text: You have the look of somebody measuring a story against a wall. Ask.
Those really were stables?
Coach stalls for the municipal school. You can see the blocked hay doors above the service roof if the security lamp catches them.
The laundry put drains through the floor. Ellery put acoustic doors over the drains and wondered why every low note travelled.

choices.text: Ask who worked in the laundry.

lines.text: Where did the sound come out?
My sink. The pub cellar. Once, a disconnected speaking tube in the borough office.
The conservatoire called those complaints evidence of exceptional resonance.
Who ran the laundry?
The baths did. Towels in through the stable yard, clean linen out under the chapel wall.
There is a painted blue line under the new tarmac. Follow it and you can read the whole building in the wrong order.
What did they practise on Thursdays?
Methods. Eight bells, same order until it was not the same order. You learned the shape without learning the name.
Near the end they rang seven and left a gap where the tenor belonged.

choices.text: Ask whether the tenor was broken.

lines.text: Was the tenor out of service?
That was the notice. But I heard it after the ringers had gone, one stroke around half past one.
A bell that size does not ring itself. That is the useful fact. The rest is neighbour talk.
When did regular practice stop?
They stopped calling it practice last winter. They did not stop doing it until April.
Words usually leave Ellery a few months before the thing they describe.
Why demolish it now?
Subsidence is the public answer. Asbestos is the answer for contractors. The council report says the stitched-together buildings cannot be separated safely.
That last one I believe. Nobody agrees where one building ends.

choices.text: Ask why it is coming down.

lines.text: Is there anything worth saving?
The foundation stone. Not because it is beautiful. Because the old name is cut deeper than every plaque they bolted over it.
Buildings should have to admit what they were first.
What would you take down first?
The enclosed bridges. Make every addition stand apart for a day and show which walls it was borrowing.
Then photograph the cracks.
Listen past the traffic. The tower always carried farther in wet weather.

lines.text: What do you hear now?
Rain in the gutter. Your van cooling. Something in Ellery holding one note below both.
You brought headphones. Use them before you decide I imagined it.
Has anyone used the stable-yard door tonight?
No. But the rain stopped striking it for a few seconds, as if somebody stood on the other side.
Neighbour talk. Remember the useful fact instead.
You with the white van? The other contractor came Tuesday, photographed the gate, and left the padlock exactly as he found it.
What other contractor?
Different name on the jacket. Same Ellery paperwork.
He did not unload anything. That is the part I remember.

lines.text: I remembered something. Ask the question you were going to ask anyway.
What did he look like?
Your height. Older or more tired. Clean orange jacket, new boots, no rain on his shoulders though it had been down all afternoon.
He carried a clipboard with no paper clipped to it.

choices.text: Ask whether the guard spoke to him.

lines.text: What company was on the jacket?
White letters. ARDEN, maybe. Or AURAL. Rain had caught the reflective strip and I read the light instead of the word.
The paperwork had your logo. I am certain of that because he kept it turned outward.
Did the lodge guard let him in?
The guard opened the sliding pane. Neither of them spoke. Then both men looked at the same empty part of the yard.
Your man shut the pane. The other one thanked him.
What was he driving?
Nothing. That was odd enough that I checked after he left.
He walked east. No taxi lamps, no bus due, no car pulling away. Just the reflective strip getting smaller.

choices.text: Ask whether cameras cover the road.

lines.text: Does the pub camera cover that road?
It covers my loading bay and one very expensive bin. Ellery made the landlord angle it away from their gate years ago.
Student privacy, they said. At half past one on a Tuesday.
No recorder case? No tools?
Clipboard, torch in his left pocket, keys heavy enough to pull the jacket crooked.
He did not unload anything. That is the part I remember.
What did he photograph?
Padlock, lodge window, your grey service door. Then he turned around and photographed the road behind himself.
Last picture was the tower. He held the phone sideways and waited long enough that it was not a picture.

choices.text: Ask what happened at the gate.

lines.text: Were the bells ringing?
Traffic, rain, bottles being tipped into the pub bin. No bell I could hear.
He lowered the phone exactly when the silence ended.
Did he touch the padlock?
No. He photographed it shut. When he walked away it swung once against the chain.
Wind can do that. There was not much wind.
He did not unload anything. That is the part I remember.

choices.text: Tell him to keep the yard clear.

lines.text: What else did you remember?
His keyring. He had a long brass key with a black tag. Your guard has the same tag hanging behind the glass.
Could be a standard set. Could be why neither man needed to speak.
Should I call the client before I go in?
If they sent him, they will tell you yes. If they did not, they will tell you no.
Ask the guard which answer makes him reach for the radio.
